each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target
distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative
uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for
all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$,
followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where
$\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to
the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite
$P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the
connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The
chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of
$\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection
restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$.
It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has
degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a
diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that
section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$. [F2, F5, step 2.2, algebra, construct]

conserved_row.complete_before_row: 4.2 The resulting sequence is still bounded in the Hilbert space $L^2(\Omega)$. Its closed linear span is separable, since rational finite linear combinations of its terms are dense. Gram–Schmidt gives a finite or countable orthonormal family with dense span. Each coordinate sequence is bounded by [F11]; repeated use of [F10] and [A1] yields a subsubsequence on which every coordinate converges. Pythagoras applied to each finite orthogonal projection bounds the sums of squared limiting coordinates by the common squared norm bound, so these coordinates define a vector $u_0$ in the closed span. Approximation by finite linear combinations proves convergence of inner products against every vector in the span. For any $z\in L^2(\Omega)$, [F12] represents $x\mapsto\langle x,z\rangle$ restricted to that span by a vector in the span, so the convergence is weak in all of $L^2$. Testing against compactly supported smooth functions shows that this weak limit and the strong $L^1$ or local-$L^1$ limit from step 4.1 define the same distribution; injectivity [F13] makes them equal almost everywhere. [A1, F10, F11, F12, F13, step 4.1, construct]

2.3 The only possible differential entries in that reduced positive-trefoil complex, by Maslov degree and the two filtration inequalities, are
$$\partial a=\alpha b,\quad\partial b=\beta Ua+\gamma c,\quad\partial c=\delta Ub,\qquad \alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta\in\mathbb F_2.$$
In its first-coordinate hat specialization the total homology is one-dimensional. If $\alpha=1$, its surviving class would be $c$ at level $-1$, contrary to step 1.2; if $\alpha=\gamma=0$, the hat homology would have rank three. Hence $\alpha=0$, $\gamma=1$. Squaring the differential gives $\delta=0$. In the other coordinate hat specialization the only possible remaining differential is $b\mapsto\beta Ua$; if $\beta=0$, it would have rank-three homology, contrary to conjugation [F5]. Thus $\beta=1$. This proves the displayed full Laurent staircase. Its dual has $\partial a^\vee=Ub^\vee$, $\partial c^\vee=b^\vee$; after $U=0$ its hat differential is exactly the displayed reverse-mirror differential. [F1, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]
